name: Divalproex Sodium
sections: Sodium hydrogen bis(2-propylpentanoate) – stable 1:1 coordination compound of sodium valproate and valproic acid
Branched short-chain fatty acid (valproate) coordination compound
White powder with a characteristic odour; insoluble in water.

Valproic acid was first synthesised in 1882 as a derivative of valeric acid; its anticonvulsant properties were discovered serendipitously in 1962. Divalproex dissociates to valproate ion in the GI tract. First approval/introduction: Valproate anticonvulsant use discovered 1962 (Pierre Eymard, France); divalproex sodium US FDA 1983 (Abbott).

Increases brain GABA levels (inhibits GABA transaminase), blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and T-type calcium currents. Stabilises neuronal membranes and mood. Receptor / target profile: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and T-type calcium channels, raises brain GABA (inhibits GABA transaminase) and inhibits histone deacetylases.
Rapidly and virtually completely absorbed (ER ~90% relative to delayed-release)
Hepatic – glucuronidation (UGT), mitochondrial beta-oxidation (>40%), minor CYP oxidation; >20 metabolites

Summary: Extended-release form gives Tmax 4–17 h. Highly protein bound (saturable). Metabolised in liver (glucuronidation, beta-oxidation). Half-life 9–16 h. Therapeutic level 50–100 µg/mL (epilepsy), 50–125 µg/mL (mania).
Acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar disorder and maintenance
Epilepsy – complex partial seizures, simple and complex absence seizures, generalised seizures (mono- or adjunctive therapy)
Prophylaxis of migraine headaches (not in women of child-bearing potential)
Mania: 25 mg/kg/day once daily, increase rapidly to clinical effect; max 60 mg/kg/day; target trough 85–125 µg/mL
Epilepsy: 10–15 mg/kg/day, increase by 5–10 mg/kg/week; max 60 mg/kg/day
Migraine: 500 mg once daily for 1 week, then 1000 mg once daily
Swallow whole once daily; monitor LFTs, platelets and levels
Pregnancy-prevention programme mandatory in females of child-bearing potential
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
No adjustment; free fraction rises in renal failure – monitor clinically.
Start lower; slower titration; monitor nutrition and somnolence.
Highest hepatotoxicity risk <2 years, especially with multiple antiepileptics or metabolic disease.
Contraindicated/avoid – major congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders. Requires specialist pregnancy-prevention measures.
Low milk levels; monitor infant for jaundice, bruising.
Hepatic disease or significant hepatic dysfunction
Pregnancy (for migraine prophylaxis) and women of child-bearing potential unless pregnancy-prevention programme in place
Hepatotoxicity – highest risk in children <2 years; monitor LFTs
Teratogenicity – neural tube defects, lower IQ; avoid in women of child-bearing potential unless no alternative
Lamotrigine – valproate doubles lamotrigine levels (halve lamotrigine dose)
Carbapenems markedly reduce valproate levels – avoid
Take with food if GI upset; swallow ER whole; avoid alcohol.
LFTs and CBC/platelets at baseline and periodically (especially first 6 months); trough levels; ammonia if lethargy/vomiting; pregnancy test.
Somnolence, coma, respiratory depression, metabolic acidosis, hypernatraemia. Supportive care; naloxone may help; haemodialysis in severe cases; L-carnitine for hyperammonaemia.
Bowden et al., JAMA 1994 – divalproex as effective as lithium in acute mania.
BALANCE (Lancet 2010) – lithium (alone or with valproate) superior to valproate alone for bipolar relapse prevention.
Women must use effective contraception and not stop suddenly if pregnant – see doctor
Report abdominal pain, vomiting, jaundice, unusual bruising
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
